concepts.name: Appointment of the Prime Minister: conventions, discretion and membership of Parliament
concepts.description: Article 75, the convention of the majority leader, presidential discretion, proof of majority and membership of the Houses.
concepts.idea: The President appoints the Prime Minister, but conventions bind the choice except where discretion arises.
concepts.rule: Article 75 says only that the President appoints the Prime Minister; by convention the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha is appointed. When no party has a clear majority, or the Prime Minister dies suddenly with no obvious successor, the President may use personal discretion (Charan Singh, 1979; Rajiv Gandhi, 1984), but must appoint the leader whom the ruling party elects. The Delhi High Court (1980) held that a majority need not be proved before appointment, and the Supreme Court (1996) allowed a non-member to be Prime Minister for six months. The Prime Minister may belong to either House, whereas in Britain the Prime Minister must be in the House of Commons (pp.308, 314).
concepts.example: Charan Singh (1979) was appointed as coalition leader and then asked to prove his majority.

concepts.name: Oath, term and salary of the Prime Minister
concepts.description: The oaths of office and secrecy, the pleasure of the President, loss of Lok Sabha confidence and the Prime Minister's pay.
concepts.idea: The Prime Minister takes two oaths, has no fixed term and is paid as Parliament determines.
concepts.rule: The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy before the Prime Minister enters office; the oath of office has four undertakings and the form is similar to that of any Union minister. The term is not fixed and the Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President, but cannot be dismissed while enjoying majority support in the Lok Sabha. On losing its confidence the Prime Minister must resign or can be dismissed (V.P. Singh 1990, Deve Gowda 1997). Salary and allowances are determined by Parliament; the Prime Minister gets those of an MP plus a sumptuary allowance, free accommodation, travelling allowance and medical facilities (pp.308-309, 314).
concepts.example: V.P. Singh resigned in 1990 after defeat in the Lok Sabha.

concepts.name: Powers of the Prime Minister over the council of ministers and other roles
concepts.description: Recommending and removing ministers, portfolios, presiding, collapse of the council, and the chairmanships and other functions.
concepts.idea: The Prime Minister heads the council: it is formed on his or her recommendation and falls with his or her resignation or death.
concepts.rule: The Prime Minister recommends the persons the President may appoint as ministers, allocates and reshuffles portfolios, and can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him or her. He or she presides over the council, guides and coordinates all ministers, and can bring about its collapse by resigning. According to the chapter, the resignation or death of the Prime Minister dissolves the council (in practice the outgoing council is usually asked to continue until a successor is sworn in); that of any other minister merely creates a vacancy. The Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog (which succeeded the Planning Commission), the National Integration Council, the Inter-State Council and the National Water Resources Council, shapes foreign policy, is chief spokesman, political-level crisis manager, party leader and political head of the services (pp.309-311).
concepts.example: A Prime Minister who differs with a minister can ask for his resignation or advise the President to dismiss him.

concepts.name: The Prime Minister in relation to the President and Parliament; Articles 74, 75, 78
concepts.description: Channel of communication, advice on appointments, leader of the Lower House and the related Articles.
concepts.idea: The Prime Minister links the President with the council and advises, rather than acts, in matters of Parliament and appointments.
concepts.rule: The Prime Minister is the principal channel of communication between the President and the council of ministers (Article 78) and advises the President, according to the chapter, on the appointment of the Attorney General, the CAG, the chairman and members of the UPSC, election commissioners and the chairman and members of the Finance Commission (since the 2023 Act, election commissioners are appointed on the recommendation of a selection committee that includes the Prime Minister). As leader of the Lower House the Prime Minister advises on summoning and proroguing sessions, can recommend dissolution of the Lok Sabha at any time, and announces government policies on the floor of the House. Article 75 provides that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President and the council is collectively responsible to the House of the People (pp.310, 312-314).
concepts.example: The Prime Minister advises the President to summon Parliament; the President summons it.

concepts.name: Role descriptions: first among equals and Prime Ministerial government
concepts.description: What Morley, Harcourt, Jennings, Laski, Greaves, Munro, Crossman, Berkely and Ambedkar said of the Prime Minister.
concepts.idea: Writers on Britain describe the Prime Minister as a dominant figure, and the chapter says the same holds good in India.
concepts.rule: Lord Morley called the Prime Minister 'primus inter pares' and 'key stone of the cabinet arch', holding a position of exceptional and peculiar authority. Harcourt called him 'a moon among lesser stars'; Jennings 'a sun around which planets revolve' with all roads leading to him; Laski the pivot of the governmental machinery, central to the cabinet's formation, life and death; Greaves the master of the Government; Munro the captain of the ship of the state. Crossman spoke of Prime Ministerial government and Berkely of the Prime Minister's super-ministerial powers; the chapter says this holds good in India, and Ambedkar compared the Prime Minister, not the President, with the US President (pp.308, 311).

concepts.name: Chief Ministers who became Prime Ministers and the caretaker government
concepts.description: The six Chief Ministers who became Prime Ministers and the meaning, limits and precedents of a caretaker government.
concepts.idea: The Constitution does not provide for a caretaker government, which may manage routine business only.
concepts.rule: Six people (Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, P.V. Narasimha Rao, H.D. Deve Gowda and Narendra Modi) became Prime Ministers after being Chief Ministers; Desai was the first non-Congress Prime Minister (March 1977) and Rao the first from South India. The Constitution contains no provision for a caretaker government; the term describes a council that has lost confidence or been dissolved but is asked to continue. It manages routine business and makes no significant policy decisions except on national security or interest. The Tarkunde Committee (1974-75), the communique of President Reddy (August 1979) and the Calcutta High Court (December 1979) support these limits (pp.312-314).
concepts.example: After the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the outgoing council cannot launch major new schemes.
